content: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) can be classified into two categories: primary pulmonary hypertension (PPH), which has no identifiable cause, and secondary pulmonary hypertension (SPH), which arises due to an underlying condition. A key feature of PH is pulmonary arteriolar vasoconstriction. Treatments for PH often focus on inducing vasodilation to alleviate this condition. Sildenafil, a vasodilator, functions by inhibiting the enzyme phosphodiesterase type V (PDE5). This review aimed to evaluate the clinical efficacy of sildenafil, administered through any route, in treating both primary and secondary forms of pulmonary hypertension. To gather relevant data, searches were conducted in MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) using predefined search terms. The search was up-to-date as of October 2006. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included in the review. Studies were selected if they assessed the effects of sildenafil in individuals with PPH or SPH. Two independent reviewers assessed and extracted data from the included clinical trials. The data were analyzed using RevMan software. Continuous data were pooled using either weighted mean difference (WMD) or standardized mean difference (SMD) scales, while dichotomous data were pooled to calculate relative risk (RR). Four studies, involving a total of 77 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Two of these studies evaluated the acute effects of sildenafil, while two small crossover studies examined the effects of long-term administration. The studies investigating acute effects demonstrated that sildenafil has a pulmonary vasodilatory effect. The crossover studies indicated improvements in symptoms, with one study specifically reporting improvements in fatigue domains based on a validated health status questionnaire. Both crossover studies also reported that sildenafil was well tolerated by participants. However, the authors noted that the validity of these findings is limited due to the small number of participants and insufficient exploration of the different underlying causes of the disease. The effects of sildenafil on long-term outcomes, such as New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class, symptoms, mortality, and exercise capacity, remain uncertain and require further investigation. Larger, well-designed studies are necessary to establish the long-term clinical benefits of sildenafil for pulmonary hypertension.
